title: Design a web crawler
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, URL frontier, politeness, dedupe, traps, recrawl.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A web crawler starts from a few seed URLs, downloads pages, extracts the links in them, and keeps going so that the pages can be indexed. Googlebot, Bingbot, Common Crawl and the crawlers behind price-comparison sites do this. The product is simple; the difficulty is doing billions of pages politely, without repeats and without getting trapped.

Functional requirements

  • Given seeds, discover and fetch pages continuously.
  • Extract text and outgoing links; store raw HTML for indexing.
  • Do not crawl the same URL twice (dedupe URLs) or store the same content twice (dedupe content).
  • Obey robots.txt and per-host rate limits (politeness).
  • Re-crawl pages periodically; recrawl news sites more often than static ones.

Non-functional requirements

  • Throughput: 1 billion pages per month (about 400 pages/s average).
  • Robust: survive slow, broken, huge or malicious pages and crawler traps.
  • Extensible: later add image, PDF or JS-rendered pages.
  • Horizontally scalable and restartable without losing progress.

Decision gravity. Choose breadth-first with priorities rather than pure depth-first. Depth-first dives into one site forever (and into traps). The frontier design is the heart of the system and is a one-way-ish door: once billions of URLs sit in it, changing its structure means a migration.

Everyday analogy. A librarian walking through a city of libraries: she notes which libraries are mentioned in each book, queues them, and never visits the same one twice in a day.

Common interview traps.

  • Not mentioning politeness and robots.txt (the first thing a real operator would ask).
  • Ignoring crawler traps (infinite calendars, session IDs in URLs).
  • Designing a single-machine queue for a billion-URL problem.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
A crawler is mostly internal, but it has three surfaces: a control API, the fetch contract, and the output feed.

POST /v1/crawl/seeds
{ "urls": ["https://news.example.com/"], "priority": "high", "recrawlEveryHours": 1 }
202 { "batchId": "b_55", "accepted": 1 }
GET /v1/crawl/status?host=news.example.com
200 { "host": "news.example.com", "queued": 18400, "fetched24h": 91233,
      "errorRate": 0.012, "crawlDelayMs": 1000, "robotsFetchedAt": "2026-11-09T06:00:00Z" }

Internal worker contract (gRPC or message): the frontier hands a lease, the fetcher returns a result.

// frontier -> fetcher (lease, 60 s)
{ "url": "https://news.example.com/a?id=7", "host": "news.example.com", "leaseId": "l_91", "depth": 3 }
// fetcher -> parser topic
{ "url": "...", "status": 200, "contentHash": "9c1f...", "blobKey": "s3://crawl/2026/11/09/9c1f.html.gz",
  "fetchedAt": "...", "etag": "W/\"abc\"" }

Output: parsed documents published to a Kafka topic crawl.pages for the search indexer.

Politeness is part of the contract: send a clear User-Agent: ExampleBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot), honour Crawl-delay and use conditional GET (If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since) on recrawl; a 304 Not Modified saves bandwidth.

Industry example. Common Crawl publishes monthly dumps (WARC files on S3); Googlebot identifies itself and obeys robots.txt.

Everyday analogy. A courier job card: leased for 60 s, returned with proof of delivery or it goes back in the queue.

Common interview traps.

  • Fetch results without leases, so a crashed worker loses URLs forever.
  • Forgetting conditional GET on recrawl.
  • No identifying User-Agent (gets blocked).

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 1B pages/month, average page 500 KB raw (about 100 KB gzipped), 10 links per page after dedupe.

Quantity Calculation Result
Fetch rate 1B / 2.6M s ~400 pages/s average, 1,000/s peak target
Bandwidth 400 x 500 KB ~200 MB/s = 1.6 Gbit/s
Raw storage / month 1B x 100 KB gzipped ~100 TB / month, ~1.2 PB / year
URLs seen 1B pages x 10 links, but heavy overlap; assume 5B unique 5B URLs
URL seen-set 5B x 8 B hash ~40 GB exact; Bloom filter at 1% FP needs ~9.6 bits/key = 6 GB
Frontier size 5B x ~100 B per URL record ~500 GB
Fetcher machines one fetcher with 500 concurrent connections, avg 1 s fetch = ~500 pages/s theoretical, 100 realistic with DNS/TLS/parsing ~10-20 fetcher nodes
DNS 1,000 lookups/s needs a local caching resolver

The bottleneck is almost never CPU; it is network latency, DNS and per-host politeness (you cannot hit one host faster than 1 request per second or so).

Industry examples. Common Crawl ingests several billion pages per month; Google's crawl is orders of magnitude larger.

Everyday analogy. A delivery fleet limited not by trucks but by how fast each customer's door can be answered.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating only bandwidth and forgetting DNS and politeness limits.
  • Storing uncompressed HTML.
  • Believing one big machine fetches 10,000 pages/s.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components:

  • URL frontier: priority queues (front) feeding per-host queues (back) so one host is served at most once per crawl-delay.
  • Fetcher workers: async HTTP clients (Netty, aiohttp, Go net/http), 500 connections each, 10 s timeout, 5 MB body cap.
  • DNS cache: local Unbound or an in-process cache, TTL honoured.
  • Robots cache: robots.txt per host cached for 24 h in Redis.
  • Parser: extracts text and links, normalises URLs, strips tracking parameters.
  • URL dedupe: Bloom filter in front of an exact store (RocksDB or Redis sharded by hash).
  • Content dedupe: SimHash or MinHash of the text to detect near-duplicates; SHA-256 of the body for exact duplicates.
  • Blob store: S3/HDFS for raw HTML; metadata in Cassandra/Bigtable keyed by URL hash.
  • Scheduler for recrawl: pushes URLs back into the frontier based on change rate.

Decision gravity: distributed frontier partitioned by host hash. Why: all URLs of one host land on one frontier shard and one fetcher group, so politeness is enforced locally with no cross-machine locks. Alternative: partition by URL hash, which spreads load evenly but means politeness requires a distributed lock per host. Breaks when one host is huge (a Wikipedia-sized site); then sub-split by host plus path bucket while sharing a rate limiter in Redis. Changing the partition scheme is a one-way door (requeue billions of URLs), so choose host hash up front.

Decision gravity: Kafka vs custom queue for the frontier. A plain Kafka topic cannot do priorities and per-host delay well. Use Kafka for the pipeline stages after fetching, and a purpose-built frontier (Redis sorted sets or a RocksDB-backed service) for scheduling. Reversible per stage.

Industry examples. Mercator (the classic paper) introduced the front/back queue frontier; Apache Nutch and StormCrawler implement the same idea; Heritrix powers the Internet Archive.

Everyday analogy. Airport check-in: many queues by priority (class), then one counter per airline that serves one passenger at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • A single global queue with no per-host structure.
  • Parsing in the fetcher thread, which blocks the network pipeline.
  • Forgetting a retry and dead-letter path.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
The URL frontier: priority and politeness

Front queues rank by PageRank-like score, update frequency and freshness need. A router maps each URL to one back queue per host; a min-heap keyed by "next allowed fetch time" tells the fetcher which host may be hit now. With crawl-delay 1 s and 400 fetches/s you need at least 400 distinct hosts active at all times; the heap guarantees that. Decision: leases with 60 s timeouts so a crashed fetcher returns its URLs automatically.

Dedupe of URLs

Normalise first: lowercase host, drop fragment #x, sort query params, remove utm_*, resolve ../, strip default ports. Then check a Bloom filter (6 GB for 5B keys at 1%); a "no" is definitive, a "yes" goes to the exact store to avoid dropping a new URL on a false positive. Alternatively accept the 1% loss for low-priority URLs. Reversible, but the Bloom filter cannot delete, so rebuild it periodically.

Content dedupe

Exact duplicate: store SHA-256(body); skip indexing if seen. Near-duplicate (same article with a different ad): SimHash 64-bit, compare Hamming distance under 3. About 30% of the web is duplicated content, so this saves index size and ranking noise.

Crawler traps and bad pages

Infinite calendars (/2026/11/10, /2026/11/11, ...), session IDs in URLs, faceted links that explode. Defences: max URL length 2,000, max depth 15, max pages per host per day, detect repeating path segments, per-host budget by importance. Cap body size at 5 MB and time at 10 s; respect Content-Type allow-list.

Robots.txt and politeness

Fetch /robots.txt first, cache 24 h; treat 4xx as "allow all", 5xx as "disallow temporarily". Obey Disallow and Crawl-delay (Google ignores crawl-delay but many crawlers honour it). Backoff on 429/503 exponentially (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... up to 1 h) per host.

Freshness: recrawl scheduling

Estimate each page's change rate from past crawls (changed in 3 of 5 visits = high). Recrawl news front pages every few minutes, product pages daily, archives monthly. Use ETag/If-Modified-Since to make unchanged recrawls cost a tiny 304. Sitemaps (sitemap.xml) give hints.

JavaScript-heavy pages

A headless browser (Chrome) renders pages but is ~10-50x costlier than a plain fetch. Route only domains flagged as client-rendered into a separate render pool. Decision is reversible per domain.

Failure handling

Fetch results go to Kafka; the parser group commits offsets after writing. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent keys (URL hash) means a retry is harmless. Dead-letter after 5 failures with the reason (DNS, TLS, timeout).

Production incident patterns. (1) The crawler hits one host at 100 req/s and takes it down: symptom is a wave of 503 and IP bans; metric: per-host request rate. (2) Frontier shard imbalance: one shard 10x larger because of a mega-host; monitor queue depth per shard. (3) A trap generates millions of unique URLs: seen-set growth rate per host spikes.

Industry examples. Googlebot's adaptive crawl rate, Common Crawl's open-source tooling, Apache Nutch on Hadoop, and Scrapy for smaller jobs.

Everyday analogy. A pollster who must not knock on the same door twice, must respect "no soliciting" signs and gives up on a street that never ends.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an exact in-memory HashSet for 5B URLs.
  • Treating a Bloom filter "yes" as certain.
  • Not normalising URLs before dedupe.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• A clear frontier with priority plus per-host politeness, and why partitioning by host works.
  • URL and content dedupe with numbers (Bloom filter size, SimHash).
  • Awareness of traps, robots.txt, timeouts and size caps.
  • Sensible estimates: pages/s, bandwidth, storage per year, fetcher count.
  • Fault tolerance via leases, at-least-once and idempotent writes.
  • Freshness strategy beyond "crawl everything again".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Crawl loop: frontier -> fetch -> parse -> dedupe -> back to frontier; store raw pages in a blob store.
  • Frontier = priority front queues plus per-host back queues enforcing crawl-delay.
  • Partition by host hash so politeness is local; this is hard to change later.
  • Dedupe: normalise URLs, Bloom filter plus exact store; SHA-256 and SimHash for content.
  • Defend against traps with depth, length, per-host budgets and body limits.
  • Recrawl by estimated change rate using conditional GETs.
  • ~400 pages/s, ~1.6 Gbit/s, ~100 TB/month compressed for 1B pages/month.

questions.subtopic: The crawl loop and why the frontier matters
questions.promptHtml: Describe the basic loop of a web crawler. Why is a plain FIFO queue not good enough for the URL frontier?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The frontier is the heart of the problem; the answer shows whether you think about priority, politeness and scale together.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The loop is: take a URL from the frontier, fetch the page, parse out text and links, dedupe the links, and put new ones back into the frontier, while storing the raw page for indexing. A single FIFO queue fails because it has no priority (news home pages matter more than a forgotten archive), no per-host politeness (it may hit one site 100 times a second), and it is a single machine's queue for billions of URLs. So the frontier is priority queues feeding per-host queues, partitioned across machines.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Seeds -> Frontier -> Fetcher -> Parser -> (Page store)
              ^                    |
              +---- dedupe <-------+
  • Breadth-first with priorities beats depth-first: depth-first dives into one site (and into traps).
  • Front queues decide what matters (PageRank-like score, change rate); back queues decide when: one queue per host and a heap keyed by next allowed fetch time.
  • With 1 s crawl-delay and 400 fetches/s you need at least 400 distinct hosts active at any moment.
  • The frontier is a near one-way door: once billions of URLs sit in it, changing its structure means a migration.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring robots.txt and per-host limits (the first question a real operator would ask).
  • A single global queue with no per-host structure.
  • Parsing in the fetcher thread, which blocks the network pipeline.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not Kafka as the frontier? -> It lacks priorities and per-host delay; use it for the stages after fetch.
  2. What if a fetcher crashes mid-job? -> Leases (60 s) return the URL to the queue automatically.
  3. How is this partitioned? -> By host hash, so politeness is enforced locally without cross-machine locks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer draws "queue, workers, DB". The senior answer designs front and back queues, leases and host partitioning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crawler built on one shared queue hammered a small site at 100 req/s and got its IP range banned.

questions.subtopic: URL dedupe with a Bloom filter
questions.contextHtml: Your crawler has seen about 5B unique URLs. A teammate proposes an in-memory HashSet<String> for dedupe. URLs average 80 bytes. You can afford roughly 10 GB of RAM across the dedupe tier. A 1% false-positive rate is acceptable for low-priority URLs.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the HashSet not work, and how would you size and use a Bloom filter?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Redis" with no numbers, or treating a Bloom "yes" as certain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we lose 1% of new URLs? Is it per priority? Do we need deletes? Does this check happen before or after normalisation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (design).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Exact storing of strings is 5B x 80 B = 400 GB (plus object overhead in Java, several times more). Storing 8-byte hashes is about 40 GB exact, still too much for 10 GB. A Bloom filter at 1% needs about 9.6 bits/key: 5B x 9.6 bits = 48 Gbit, about 6 GB, with about 7 hash functions.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute the formula, then run a load test of insert and lookup at 1,000 URLs/s; measure the real false-positive rate.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The decision is that a "no" is definitive and a "yes" is only probable.
  6. Fix: Normalise first (lowercase host, drop fragment and utm_*, sort query, strip default port), check the Bloom filter, and on "yes" confirm in an exact store (RocksDB or sharded Redis) for high-priority URLs; accept the 1% loss for low-priority ones.
  7. Prevention: A Bloom filter cannot delete, so rebuild it periodically (for example per epoch); monitor fill ratio since the false-positive rate rises as it fills.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not drop new URLs silently for important sites; verify those in the exact store. I would not shard the filter without hash-by-host consistency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the target FP rate is 0.1%? -> About 14.4 bits/key, roughly 9 GB.
  • What if the set doubles to 10B? -> Filter must be resized and rebuilt; plan for growth or use scalable Bloom filters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A crawler never re-found a cluster of pages because the filter had filled beyond its design size; FP rate had silently climbed to 20%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: HashSet or hand-waves.
  • Hire: Numbers (6 GB), "no is definitive", exact fallback.
  • Strong hire: Normalisation, fill monitoring, rebuild plan.

questions.subtopic: Politeness with front and back queues
questions.promptHtml: How does a crawler stay polite to each website while still fetching 400+ pages per second?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Politeness is a hard constraint that shapes the data structure. It separates people who have thought about the real system.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Politeness means never hitting a host faster than its crawl delay, and obeying robots.txt. I use front queues ordered by importance and back queues, one per host. A min-heap keyed by "next allowed fetch time" tells fetchers which host may be hit now. Because 400 fetches/s with a 1 s delay needs at least 400 distinct hosts active, the heap ensures workers always have a ready host. I partition the frontier by host hash so one machine owns a host and no distributed lock is needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
New URLs -> Prioritizer -> Front queue (high/low) -> Router -> Back queue per host -> Fetcher
Heap: (host A, next=12:00:01.2), (host B, next=12:00:00.4) ...
  • Robots.txt is fetched first and cached for 24 h; 4xx means allow all, 5xx means disallow for now.
  • On 429 or 503 apply per-host exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... up to 1 h).
  • Send an identifying User-Agent with a contact URL; use conditional GET on recrawl.
  • If one host is huge (Wikipedia-sized), a per-host limit is still enforced, maybe with a higher rate agreed by policy.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Per-URL partitioning that spreads one host over many machines without a shared limiter.
  • Forgetting that DNS and TLS time also consume your per-host budget.
  • Treating crawl-delay as mandatory for all bots (some search engines ignore it); decide your own policy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if all workers are idle waiting for hosts? -> Too few active hosts; widen the priority mix.
  2. How do you handle a site with a 10 s crawl-delay and 10M pages? -> Budget by importance; it will take a long time; do not break the rule.
  3. How do you share limits when sub-splitting a mega host? -> A shared rate limiter in Redis keyed by host.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "add a sleep". The senior answer designs the heap, host partitioning and backoff policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fetch fleet scaled to 200 workers produced 100 req/s on one host and caused 503s and an IP ban.

questions.contextHtml:
A site owner emails you: your bot took their server down. Your logs:

host: shop.example.org   requests/min: 6,300   (105 req/s)   status 503: 38%   avg latency 4.1 s
frontier shard 3: host queue depth 2.1M   lease timeouts: 9,800/h
robots.txt for host: fetched 3 days ago, Crawl-delay: 2

You had recently increased the fetcher fleet from 20 to 80 workers and moved from host-hash to URL-hash partitioning "for better balance".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a rate limiter to the fetcher", without noticing the partitioning change broke the central assumption.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the limiter live per worker or per host globally? When was robots.txt cached last and did it change? How many workers could pick this host simultaneously?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the host in the frontier now, email the owner, and set a hard ceiling (for instance 1 req/2 s) before resuming. Honour their contact preference.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) URL-hash partitioning let all 80 workers pull URLs for the same host at once, each applying its own local delay, so aggregate rate was about 80 x 0.5 = 40+ req/s and more. (b) Robots.txt cache stale (3 days versus a 24 h policy). (c) Lease timeouts caused retries, adding load on a struggling host. (d) 503 responses did not trigger backoff.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-host request-rate dashboard, which workers fetched this host, backoff logs, robots fetch time, retry counts.
  5. Root cause: Politeness was enforced per worker, not per host, after partitioning by URL.
  6. Fix: Return to host-hash partitioning so one owner enforces the delay, or keep URL partitioning with a distributed per-host rate limiter. Enforce exponential backoff on 429/503, refresh robots every 24 h, cap per-host concurrency to 1.
  7. Prevention: Alert on per-host rate above the delay; a test that simulates 80 workers against a stub host and asserts max rate; code review checklist for crawlers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not give up balance; the mega-host problem is solved by sub-splitting plus a shared limiter, not by dropping host ownership. Changing partitioning again is a one-way door that requeues billions of URLs, so make the decision with care.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the owner wants less traffic? -> Respect the request, lower the budget for the host, and record it.
  • Is blocking by IP a concern? -> Yes; being identifiable and polite avoids it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scale-up doubled the worker count and quietly broke an assumption that only one worker would ever hold a given host. Per-host rate went from 1/s to 40/s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds sleeps.
  • Hire: Finds partitioning/limiter mismatch, backoff, robots refresh.
  • Strong hire: Global per-host limits, tests with many workers, alerts and communication with the owner.

questions.contextHtml:
Dashboards show the seen-set growing 3x faster than usual, with fetch throughput flat:

host: events.example.net   new_urls/hour: 4.2M   distinct_pages (content hash): 1,900
sample urls:
  /calendar/2031/04/17?view=month&session=a81f
  /calendar/2031/04/18?view=month&session=c92b
  /calendar/2031/04/19?view=month&session=e07d
frontier depth for host: 14 -> 4,100
questions.promptHtml: What is this, and how do you stop it and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Block that host", which fixes one instance and not the class of problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this one host or many? Does the content hash vary? How much of the fetch budget is this host consuming?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Apply a per-host page budget and pause the host's expansion; strip session parameters so URLs normalise.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: An infinite calendar plus a session ID in the URL creates unbounded unique URLs; low distinct-content ratio (1,900 pages out of millions of URLs) confirms it. Alternatives: a faceted-search explosion or a link generator bug.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group new URLs by path pattern and parameter set; compute the ratio of distinct content hashes to URLs; look for repeating segments.
  5. Root cause: No defences against unbounded link spaces: depth, budget, or normalisation.
  6. Fix: Normalise: drop session and tracking parameters. Limits: max URL length 2,000, max depth 15, max pages per host per day scaled by importance, detect repeating path segments, a distinct-content ratio check that throttles hosts producing many new URLs but few new pages. Body cap 5 MB and 10 s timeout.
  7. Prevention: Alert on seen-set growth per host; dashboard of unique content ratio per host; regression tests on a trap fixture site.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not set budgets so low that legitimate large sites (marketplaces) are cut off; budgets scale with host importance. Dropping calendar paths by hand does not generalise.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the trap is hidden behind JavaScript? -> The render pool needs the same budgets.
  • What about SimHash? -> Helps near-duplicate detection at content level, but the URL budget protects the frontier before fetch.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single forum with session IDs in links consumed a double-digit percentage of one shard's frontier before anyone noticed. Normalisation rules fixed it in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blocklists the host.
  • Hire: Normalises, adds depth/budget limits.
  • Strong hire: Uses content-hash ratio as a signal, monitoring and a trap test fixture.

questions.contextHtml: The crawler works at 1B pages per month (about 400 pages/s average, 1,000/s peak). The business now wants 10B pages per month with the same freshness policy. Average page 500 KB raw, about 100 KB gzipped. Fetcher nodes realistically reach about 100 pages/s each.
questions.promptHtml: What numbers change, what breaks first, and what do you redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add 10x machines." It ignores politeness, DNS, storage growth and the seen-set.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 10x spread across more hosts or deeper on the same hosts? Same recrawl ratio? Budget for storage and bandwidth?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (planning).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Politeness becomes the limit: 4,000 pages/s at 1 s delay needs 4,000+ distinct hosts active. DNS: 4,000 lookups/s needs a caching resolver fleet. Seen-set and frontier grow 10x.
  4. How I'd verify each: Fetch rate: 10B / 2.6M s = about 3,850/s average, 10,000/s peak. Bandwidth: 4,000 x 500 KB = 2 GB/s = 16 Gbit/s. Storage: 10B x 100 KB = about 1 PB/month, 12 PB/year compressed. URLs seen: about 50B; Bloom at 1% needs 9.6 bits x 50B = 60 GB; frontier 50B x 100 B = 5 TB. Fetcher nodes: 4,000 / 100 = about 40 at average, about 100 at peak.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The costs that grow slowest relative to value are CPU; the ones that bite are storage, bandwidth bills, the frontier, and host diversity.
  6. Fix: Shard the frontier and Bloom filters by host hash with more shards; local DNS caches per fetcher group; tiered storage (hot recent, cold archive) and more aggressive content dedupe (SimHash saves around 30% of duplicated content); prioritise by importance rather than crawling everything; sample low-value hosts.
  7. Prevention: Per-shard queue depth, per-host budgets, bandwidth and storage cost dashboards, a capacity review each quarter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not scale fetchers before checking that enough distinct hosts exist; otherwise workers idle. I would not store uncompressed HTML.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if it must be 10x fresher instead of 10x bigger? -> Recrawl budget by change rate, conditional GETs (304s cost tiny), sitemaps for hints.
  • Cost? -> Egress and storage dominate; compress and tier.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team scaled fetchers 5x and saw throughput rise only 1.5x. The frontier had too few active hosts; workers waited for their hosts' delay timers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Linear scaling only.
  • Hire: Redoes the numbers and notes the Bloom/frontier growth.
  • Strong hire: Identifies host diversity and DNS limits, tiered storage and prioritisation.

questions.contextHtml:
Frontier partitioning is by host hash across 64 shards. One shard holds 10x the queued URLs of the others because a single large site (tens of millions of pages) landed on it.

shard 17: queued 410M   fetch rate 12/s   oldest URL age 19 days
shard 18: queued 38M    fetch rate 110/s  oldest URL age 2 hours

The big site allows only 1 request/second per the crawl delay and this is correct policy.
questions.promptHtml: Is this a bug? What do you change, and what is the decision gravity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Re-shard by URL hash", which breaks politeness and requeues everything.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the low rate the policy ceiling (1/s for the host)? Are other hosts on shard 17 starved? Is the host important enough to deserve more budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the other hosts off shard 17 by remapping (small hosts rebalance cheaply) so they are not starved by the mega-host.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Not a bug for the big site: its rate is bounded by the crawl delay. (b) It is a bug for the small hosts sharing the shard if one big site's queue crowds them. (c) The shard also needs memory for 410M entries.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-host rate and age on shard 17; per-host queue depth; memory and disk on the shard.
  5. Root cause: Host-hash partitioning gives load skew when host sizes are heavy-tailed.
  6. Fix: Sub-split mega hosts by host plus path bucket into several queues owned by different shards, with a shared per-host rate limiter in Redis so the aggregate stays at 1 req/s (or the agreed higher rate). Give important hosts a larger budget; prune low-value URLs on the big site with a frontier budget instead of queuing 410M of them.
  7. Prevention: Alert on queue-depth skew per shard and oldest-URL age; a policy for heavy hosts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Changing the base partition scheme is a one-way door: it requeues billions of URLs and loses the local politeness property. Sub-splitting only the exceptions is a smaller, reversible step. I would not exceed the host's crawl delay to "catch up".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the site gives permission for 20 req/s? -> Spread across shards with a shared limiter at 20/s.
  • Could we drop most of its URLs? -> Yes, importance-based budgets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A forum host with 200M URLs pinned one shard for months. It turned out 90% of its URLs were sort-order variants and were safely dropped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Re-shard by URL.
  • Hire: Notes policy-bound rate, sub-splits the exception, shared limiter.
  • Strong hire: Budgeting/pruning, per-shard skew alerts and the one-way-door framing.

questions.contextHtml: Product now needs news sites updated within 5 minutes and a set of 20,000 e-commerce domains that render content client-side with JavaScript. Currently every page is recrawled on a fixed 7-day cycle with a plain HTTP fetch. A headless browser render costs about 10-50x a plain fetch. The budget allows 20% more compute.
questions.promptHtml: How do you meet the requirement without blowing the budget?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Render everything in headless Chrome and recrawl everything every 5 minutes."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which exact domains are news? What does "updated" mean (new article discovered, or any change)? Is a headline-level snapshot enough? Can we use sitemaps/RSS feeds?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (design).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Freshness should be driven by estimated change rate per page, not a global timer. Rendering is needed only for domains whose raw HTML lacks the content.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure change rate from past crawls (changed in 3 of 5 visits = high); test each e-commerce domain for content in raw HTML versus rendered DOM; check sitemaps and feeds.
  5. Root cause: A uniform policy wastes budget on static pages while starving hot ones.
  6. Fix: Recrawl scheduler with per-page change-rate estimate: news home and section pages every few minutes, product pages daily, archives monthly. Use conditional GET so unchanged recrawls cost a tiny 304. Discover new articles through RSS and sitemaps instead of re-crawling heavy pages. A separate render pool only for domains flagged client-rendered, with limited concurrency and a per-domain quota; cache rendering results and prefer a site's JSON endpoint where available.
  7. Prevention: Per-class freshness SLO dashboards (age of newest crawl by class), render cost per domain, an alert when render share exceeds the budget.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not run all pages through Chrome; it is reversible per domain, so start with the top domains by traffic. I would not recrawl static pages every 5 minutes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the site has no sitemap and changes constantly? -> Poll the listing page frequently and fetch only new links.
  • Politeness for 5-minute news polling? -> Fewer pages, still obey delay; polling one index page is cheap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team rendered all e-commerce pages and ran out of budget in a week; only 12% of domains actually needed rendering.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Brute force.
  • Hire: Change-rate-based recrawl, conditional GET, render only when needed.
  • Strong hire: Sitemaps/feeds discovery, per-class SLOs and cost caps for render pool.
